**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

No checklist line is answered no. The heading line was unsure, but after the deep read it is yes: the H1 describes the article's topic, which is what the "Headings and labels" rule (WCAG 2.4.6) checks. Two copy findings have no checklist line, and I'm passing them on for the director to rank:

1. **The page promises a how-to but never says how (no checklist line).**
   - **Where:** The H1 at 380–915 px x, 135–210 px y reads "Update the card that pays for your subscription". The sidebar item "Update a payment card" at about 96, 178 px points to the same page.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The first paragraph says only "You can replace the card on file at any time from the billing page". The page has no steps (where the billing page is, which button to press, what to confirm), and "the billing page" isn't a link, although three side topics are. The second paragraph even sends invoice payers to "follow the steps in paying by invoice", which shows that this page has no steps of its own. Someone who came to change their card leaves knowing the rules around the change but not how to make it. They will probably go hunting through the app or open a ticket.
   - **Why:** Common sense for task-based help content.
   - **Fix:** Put a short numbered procedure right under the H1, starting with a link to the billing page. Move the timing rules and the permissions paragraph below it.
   - Defect. Major.

2. **The decline-retry schedule can be read two ways, and it decides when the plan is downgraded (no checklist line).**
   - **Where:** The paragraph under "When the new card is declined", 380–1050 px x, 515–620 px y.
   - **What the viewer meets:**
     - "after three days and after seven days" doesn't say what the days are counted from. It could be the first decline or the previous retry, which would put the second retry at day 7 or day 10.
     - "after the second attempt" could mean the first retry (the second charge in total) or the second retry (day 7).
     - So a customer can't tell whether they have about 3 or about 7 days, or longer, to add a working card before the workspace drops to the free plan.
   - **Why:** Deadline copy that can be read two ways is a defect.
   - **Fix:** State dates against one anchor, for example: "We retry 3 days and 7 days after the first decline. If both retries fail, your subscription moves to the free plan on day 7."
   - Defect. Major.

**What's working.**
- The H1 is a full sentence in the customer's own terms ("the card that pays for your subscription"), not a product label. The subhead "When the new card is declined" names exactly the case it covers, so a scanning reader finds the failure case without reading the body.
- Type, colour and rules all have the same plain, quiet tone, with one link style and no ornament. Nothing on the page competes with the text, which suits a help article.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The H1 at about 30 px bold (x 380–912, y 135–210) is the only large element on the page. With the logo, nav and sidebar kept small and regular, a visitor knows in under a second which article they're on.
- The subhead "When the new card is declined" (y ≈ 487) is only slightly larger than the body. The bold weight and the extra space above it (about 40 px, against about 12 px below) mark it as a heading, so it doesn't need another big size step. That follows Refactoring UI's "bolder, not bigger". The spacing also ties the subhead to its own paragraph, so a reader scanning for the decline case finds it at once.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. This is a single-screen help-article page (1280×800), so I judged it from the whole image. No measured facts file was given, so the pixel values below are estimates by eye.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No, at one point: the space above the H2 "When the new card is declined" (y≈487). The heading itself is placed correctly. It sits closer to its own paragraph (≈38 px, text centre to centre) than to the paragraph above (≈53 px). The problem is that the space above it is only about 6 px more than the normal gap between the first two paragraphs (≈47 px, y≈331 to 378). So the page's one section break gets almost the same space as a paragraph break. Only the heading's bold weight tells the reader a new topic starts. Scanning the page, the reader sees three evenly spaced paragraph blocks rather than an intro followed by a separate section about a declined card. That is the section a worried reader is scanning for. The rule (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II, on proximity) is that the gap between groups must be clearly larger than the gap within a group. Fix: make the space above H2s clearly larger than the paragraph gap. Roughly double the paragraph gap is a good target. Keep the space below the H2 tight, as it is now. Convention. Weight: minor. It costs little on a page this short, but the problem grows with each section a longer article adds.

**What's working.**
- **Alignment is strict.** The logo and sidebar share one left edge (x≈96). The breadcrumb, H1, body and H2 share another (x≈380). The sidebar label "In this section" and the breadcrumb line up at the same height (y≈113). Nothing is a few pixels off, so the page looks deliberately built. Keep these two left edges and the shared top line when adding content.
- **Empty space is gathered, not scattered.** The open space falls into large areas: below the short sidebar list, to the right of the text column, and below the article. The text column itself stays dense, which gives the body copy a calm frame and makes the article the clear thing to look at.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (space inside each group clearly smaller than between groups)

I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts because Bash is denied in this session. The screenshot is only 1280×800, so I worked from the whole image and read the reference entries with the Read tool instead.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters? No.** The body column runs from about x=380 to x=1050. At about 17 px type the lines come to roughly 82–85 characters. For example, "You can replace the card on file at any time from the billing page. The new card is" is about 83 characters, and "We try a declined card again after three days and after seven days, and we send an" is about 82. That is above the 45–75 range and the ideal of about 66 (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.1.2). The overrun is small and the generous line spacing (about 28 px) offsets it, so a reader is unlikely to lose their place on these short paragraphs. Each line is still a little long to scan comfortably. **Fix:** narrow the text column to about 600 px, or about 66 characters at this size. The page has plenty of empty space on the right (x≈1050–1280) to absorb it. **Convention. Weight: minor.**
2. **Copy, not a checklist line: "If the card is still declined after the second attempt" can be read two ways.** This is in the last paragraph, around y=553–581. The paragraph lists two retries, at three days and at seven days. "Second attempt" could mean the second charge overall, which is the 3-day retry, or the second retry, which is the 7-day one. The difference decides when the workspace drops to the free plan. That is a date the customer will act on and later hold the company to. A reader who takes the first meaning expects a downgrade four days earlier than one who takes the second, and one of them will be wrong. **Fix:** name the day, for example "If the card is still declined on the seven-day retry, your subscription moves to the free plan." That also says it to the reader with "your." **Defect. Weight: major** for a billing help article, because this is the line people act on.

**What's working.**
- **Clear type scale.** One sans family with clear steps: a heading of about 32 px with tight leading that reads as one unit, a bold subhead of about 19 px, and 17 px body with about 28 px leading. The body text is larger than the nav (about 15 px) and the sidebar (about 14 px). The text reads as plainly the main content without any decoration.
- **Easy-to-scan paragraphs.** Short paragraphs, flush left, separated by space with no indents. A real subhead ("When the new card is declined") lets a reader jump straight to the failure case.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters)

sections.report:
I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts because Bash was blocked in this mode. The image is about one screen, so I worked from the whole image, and I read the entries in `references/ux.md` with Read instead.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has navigation links, a breadcrumb and links in the body text, but no buttons or form fields.

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them, instead of making them hunt for it?** and **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?** The page's job is the H1, "Update the card that pays for your subscription". The only directions are "from the billing page" in the first paragraph (about x 900–1035, y 247). That phrase isn't a link and doesn't say where the billing page is. Below it there are no steps and no "Go to billing" link or button. The reader learns the rules about invoices, roles and declined cards, but has to leave and find the actual control on their own, which is the one thing they came for.
   - Why: Nielsen 6, recognition rather than recall. The anticipation point is common sense, since its only source, Tognazzini, isn't on the approved list.
   - Fix: link "the billing page" straight to the place where the card is changed. Better still, give the task as a short numbered set of steps, or one prominent "Go to billing" link near the top. Then the next action sits in front of the reader before the edge cases.
   - Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does the screen show where the user is?** The "In this section" sidebar (x 96–251, y 147–271) draws "Update a payment card" exactly like its four siblings. The top nav draws "Billing" (x 792, y 30) like the other three items. The small grey breadcrumb at y 113 is the only sign of location, so someone who arrived from search can't see at a glance which article in the list they're reading or what's next to it.
   - Why: Nielsen 1, and Laubheimer, "Menu-Design Checklist" (NN/g), guideline 5.
   - Fix: mark the current page in the navigation with one clear cue, such as a bolder weight, a bar or underline, or a background, so the reader can see where they are. Do this on the sidebar item, and ideally on "Billing" in the top nav too.
   - Convention. Weight: minor.
3. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search?** The help-centre header (y 0–63) holds only the "Ledgerly Help" wordmark and four topic links. There's no search field anywhere on the page. Searching is how most people get around a help centre. Without it, a reader whose question isn't one of the five sidebar titles has to guess which of the four topics holds the answer.
   - Why: Nielsen 7. Search is also the expected pattern for a help centre (Jakob's law).
   - Fix: put a search field in the header, or at the top of the article column.
   - Convention. Weight: minor for this article page. It would be major across the help centre as a whole.

**What's working.**
- The links in the body text ("check your billing history", "roles and permissions", "paying by invoice", "restore your previous plan") are blue and underlined, so they're marked by more than colour. Each link's text names where it goes, so the reader knows what they'll get before clicking.
- The structure is clear: four topic areas in the top nav, an "In this section" list of sibling articles, and a breadcrumb. A first-time reader can tell how the help content is organised.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the links, especially the grey breadcrumb "Billing" and the sidebar items, show a visible focus indicator. Check this in a browser with the keyboard.
- Whether the header is sticky and covers focused links when the page scrolls.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 27 yes, 4 no (shows where the user is; nothing to remember from another screen; shortcuts such as search; puts what the user needs next in front of them), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not covered)
